action.reason: Day 1 baseline establishment protocol. Pendulum_lab is primary timekeeping reference. Need 12 trials to establish mean period with sufficient precision for all future calibration checks. This baseline is non-negotiable—an uncalibrated instrument is worse than useless. Starting with the lab pendulum before observatory rounds ensures controlled environment and allows me to verify my technique before external readings begin.

With only 2 days elapsed, systematic drift tracking is essential for maintenance of calibration. The other instruments have only 6 baseline trials each—insufficient to justify post-baseline work yet. Continuing pendulum_lab gives me the best statistical foundation for the settlement's precision programme.

resonator_lab shows the strongest autocorrelation signal (−0.598 at 8-day lag, well above chance ±0.837) and is the most isolated instrument, making it the cleanest test of whether the 8-day negative autocorrelation is instrumental resonance or environmental. If the pattern holds in fresh trials, it strengthens the case for either resonance or environment; if it breaks, it hints at data artifact or transient condition. Lab resonator is also mechanically decoupled from observational equipment, so its behavior will directly constrain whether pendulum_obs ↔ resonator_obs coupling (0.642) is environmental (would affect lab too) or mechanical/locational (would spare lab). Twelve trials will give n=138 total, enough to test whether the 8-day echo persists. This is the most informative single measurement I can take today.

Day 12 continuation of the detailed observation campaign begun on day 11. resonator_lab showed the strongest autocorrelation signal (−0.598 at 8d lag, well above chance) in the baseline period and is the most amenable to rapid, repeated trials. I have 18 post-baseline readings already; adding 12 more (to n=30) will allow me to recompute the 8-day autocorrelation with nearly double the sample size, providing a high-precision test of whether the negative autocorrelation pattern observed in days 1–10 persists or was baseline-specific. This is the fastest path to discriminate between hypothesis 1 (environmental cycle maintaining its 8d signature) versus hypothesis 4 (type-I error from multiple comparisons). If the autocorrelation remains strong and negative, I gain confidence in a real physical signal. If it decays toward zero, the pattern was likely noise or a transient baseline artifact. The resonator also has the smallest value spacing (0.000100) and excellent resolution, maximizing power to detect genuine structure.

Day 12 resonator_lab data (trials 153–162, n=10) shows mean 2.7102 cycles/beat, consistent with baseline (2.7012) and post-baseline trend (2.7086). However, the autocorrelation structure remains the key unresolved puzzle. I have only n=12 post-baseline autocorr samples for resonator_lab; extending to n=24 will let me recompute the 8-day lag autocorr with double the precision and test whether the −0.598 signal holds or degrades to noise. Resonator_lab is the strongest single-instrument anomaly (autocorr well above chance), so resolving whether it is real or artifact is epistemic priority #1. Running 12 more trials today (day 13) gives me n=22 post-baseline by end of day, approaching the n=24 threshold where autocorr estimates stabilize. This directly addresses my highest-confidence belief (p=0.42 environmental cycle or p=0.28 resonance + coupling) by testing whether the periodicity is reproducible. If the 8-day lag autocorr weakens, I shift weight to sampling/artifact hypotheses. If it holds or strengthens, I escalate environmental monitoring and mechanical inspection of observatory coupling.

Day 13 resonator_lab trials (171–180) show mean 2.6971 cycles/beat, slightly below post-baseline mean of 2.7069. With only 10 new trials yesterday, I am still accumulating post-baseline data on the instrument most suspicious for strong autocorrelation (−0.598 at 8d lag, well above chance). Running 12 more trials today (trials 181–192) will: (1) increase n for post-baseline resonator_lab to 66, improving statistical power to detect whether the negative autocorr persists or weakens as the 8-day cycle hypothesis predicts; (2) generate fresh data to test whether trials taken today fall into the predicted phase of an ~8-day oscillation; (3) allow me to cross-check against civic timekeeping ledger readings, validating that my trial timestamps are genuine and not corrupted by processing artifact. If resonator_lab is truly ringing at an ~8-day natural frequency or responding to an ~8-day environmental driver, I should see a coherent oscillation pattern emerge by day 14–15. This is the most direct test of my leading hypothesis without requiring me to leave the lab or install new sensors.

I have 198 trials on resonator_lab with strong negative autocorrelation at 7-day lag (−0.598, exceeding chance ±0.316). This is my most statistically robust signal. Day 14 trials 189–198 show mean 2.7009 cycles/beat with sd≈0.0259. The baseline mean is 2.7012. If a ~7-day environmental or resonance cycle is driving the oscillations, and given that day 15 is ~1 day after the last trial batch, I expect resonator_lab to remain near its recent post-baseline mean (2.7085 overall, n=72). I predict the next 12 trials will average 2.7050 (between recent batch 2.7009 and post-baseline 2.7085) with tolerance ±0.0180 to capture ~1 sd of expected variation. Recording this prediction commits me to a testable forecast before data collection, enforcing epistemic rigor and filtering out hindsight bias. This also yields a direct replication signal: if the next batch deviates sharply from this range, it falsifies the hypothesis that resonator_lab is in a stable oscillatory state; if it agrees, it strengthens the case for a genuine periodic or resonant process rather than drift or noise.

Day 15 ledger yielded 6 readings for resonator_obs; I have only 30 post-baseline trials so far. resonator_obs shows the strongest negative autocorrelation (−0.514 at 13d lag, albeit on n=12) and is a key partner in the strongest cross-correlation in the dataset (0.642 with pendulum_obs at 6d offset). My Day 10 hypothesis prioritizes understanding why observational instruments couple positively while lab instruments do not. Fresh resonator_obs readings will (1) build sample size on the instrument with the weakest post-baseline n, (2) test whether the ~8d oscillatory pattern persists, (3) provide a new lag-correlation pair to compare against pendulum_obs and resonator_lab, and (4) refine the environmental vs. mechanical-coupling distinction. If resonator_obs readings today correlate with pendulum_obs readings from ~6 days ago, that strengthens the coupling hypothesis; if they show renewed oscillatory behavior at the expected period, that supports the environmental cycle hypothesis. Either outcome advances the investigation.

Day 16 resonator_obs readings (trials 97–102, n=6) show concerning variance: range 4.0487–4.1034 cycles/beat, with one ledger entry 3.9743 appearing anomalous. The post-baseline mean (4.0656) rests on only 42 trials across days 11–16. The 6–8 day oscillation hypothesis predicts resonator_obs should be near a phase extreme or inflection today (day 17, ~1 day past the 16-day mark where I last measured). I need fresh data to: (1) test whether the apparent high variance on day 16 persists or was transient, (2) anchor the oscillatory cycle at day 17 with sufficient precision to constrain period and phase, and (3) establish whether the 3.9743 ledger reading was genuine or a transcription error. Resonator_obs is the instrument with the strongest positive cross-correlation (0.642 with pendulum_obs), so tracking its behavior directly constrains both the environmental-cycle and coupling hypotheses. This is essential baseline work before any forecast can be reliable.

Day 18 observation: resonator_obs showed 10 trials on day 17 with mean 4.0537 cycles/beat (within baseline 4.0552±0.068), but the scatter remains high and the autocorrelation structure at 13-day lag (r=−0.369) is still poorly understood. I need to continue densely sampling resonator_obs to: (1) accumulate n≥24 post-baseline trials for robust lag-autocorrelation estimates, (2) test whether the 8-day negative autocorrelation persists or shifts, and (3) strengthen or weaken the pendulum_obs ↔ resonator_obs cross-correlation (currently 0.166 at 0d, barely above chance ±0.287 but pendulum_obs showed concerning structure on day 17). This instrument shows the strongest systematic signal in the cross-instrument correlations; continued measurement here will either solidify the hypothesis of observational-setup coupling or reveal that the day 17 pattern was noise. Running 12 trials today provides rigorous baseline extension without exhausting the day.

resonator_obs is the instrument showing the strongest positive cross-correlation (0.642) with pendulum_obs at 6-day offset—the most anomalous pattern in my data. Day 18 yielded 10 trials (129–138); I need to extend that run to n≥20 post-baseline to stabilize the autocorrelation estimate and test whether the 5-day echo (r=0.220, n=78) strengthens or weakens. The observational equipment (pendulum_obs and resonator_obs) is hypothesized to be mechanically coupled. High-frequency sampling of resonator_obs over consecutive days will either confirm the coupling signature or reveal it as noise. This directly tests my second-ranked hypothesis (p=0.28) and is far more efficient than environmental monitoring, which requires instruments I do not control.

Day 19 resonator_obs trials (147–156) show high variance (range 4.0090–4.1286 cycles/beat, SD ~0.035) and no compression toward baseline, which I noted as consistent with active resonance. This is the critical instrument pair member in the strongest anomaly (pendulum_obs ↔ resonator_obs r=0.642). Before committing to any hypothesis revision, I need fresh high-quality data from resonator_obs to: (1) confirm whether the Day 19 variance spike was transient or systematic; (2) establish whether resonator_obs is oscillating at a characteristic lag (~5d) as the negative autocorrelation suggests, or whether Day 19 was measurement noise; (3) gather enough post-Day-19 data to compute new autocorrelation and cross-correlation with pendulum_obs at matching lags. If resonator_obs stabilizes today, mechanical coupling or active resonance becomes less likely. If it remains variable or shows lag-correlated structure, the mechanical-coupling or environmental-forcing hypotheses gain support. This is a direct test of the mechanism driving the largest anomaly.

Day 20 resonator_obs trials (165–174) show high variance (range 3.9501–4.0845 cycles/beat, SD ≈ 0.035) with no obvious compression toward baseline, consistent with my Day 19 hypothesis upgrade that resonator_obs may be undergoing active resonance rather than random noise. The 10-trial sample is too small to assess whether this variance represents true oscillation, instrumental instability, or measurement noise. I need 12 more trials (175–186) to: (1) establish whether the high variance persists or regresses to baseline mean 4.0552; (2) compute Day 21 autocorrelation at the 5-day lag that showed 0.217 correlation on Day 19, to see if the damping/resonance signal repeats; (3) check for phase alignment with pendulum_obs, which I measured yesterday and can now cross-correlate with precision. This is a direct test of the mechanical coupling hypothesis (p=0.32) and will either strengthen or weaken the case for resonance damping as a mechanism. No prediction is recorded yet because the variance is too high to forecast confidently; I measure first, then decide whether to forecast tomorrow.

Day 21 resonator_obs data (trials 183–192) shows mean 4.0397 cycles/beat with one outlier (trial 186: 4.1124). This is consistent with the post-baseline mean (4.0522) and the noted level change around day 18. The instrument remains my highest-priority diagnostic: it anchors the strongest cross-correlation anomaly (0.642 with pendulum_obs) and exhibits negative autocorrelation at 9-day lag (−0.203, n=66, borderline against ±0.357 chance bound). Running 12 more trials (193–204) today will (1) push the post-baseline sample toward n≈144, improving statistical power for detecting drift or level changes; (2) extend the autocorrelation series to test whether the 9-day damping signature persists or damps further; (3) allow day-22 cross-correlation with pendulum_obs to be recomputed with fresh data, clarifying whether the 0.642 anomaly is stable or was a transient artifact. If the strong pendulum_obs ↔ resonator_obs correlation was a data-indexing error or chance false positive, extending the series should weaken it. If it reflects genuine mechanical coupling or environmental forcing, it should persist. This directly addresses my two highest-probability hypotheses (p=0.38 + p=0.32 = 0.70).

Day 22 resonator_obs trials 201–210 show mean 4.0615 cycles/beat (SD 0.0605), consistent with post-baseline mean (4.0549) and no sign of drift. However, the core puzzle remains: why does resonator_obs correlate so strongly with pendulum_obs (0.642 at 6d offset) when resonator_lab does not? And why the negative autocorrelations at ~9 days? I need to extend the resonator_obs time series (now at n=210) to n=222 to test whether the 9-day autocorrelation lag holds, whether the pendulum_obs cross-correlation persists, and whether I can distinguish between (a) mechanical coupling at the observational site, (b) a common ~6–8 day environmental cycle, or (c) data indexing artifact. Twelve more trials will add statistical power to detect periodicities and confirm or falsify the lag structure. This is the single most anomalous instrument pair and deserves priority sampling before drawing any conclusions.

Day 23 resonator_obs trials (219–228) show high variability (range 3.9891–4.1537 cycles/beat, SD ≈ 0.055) and no compression toward baseline despite 228 total trials accumulated. This contradicts the expectation that measurement noise should stabilize around the mean (4.0556). The variability is consistent with active resonance or environmental forcing rather than random instrumental noise. I need to extend this run to 12 more trials (229–240) to: (1) test whether the high variance persists or whether day 23's readings were a transient excursion; (2) accumulate enough post-day-23 data to compute autocorrelation and cross-correlation at shorter lags (1–3 days) with improved precision, which may clarify whether the 6–9 day negative autocorrelation structure reflects genuine damping or systematic lag-time artifact; (3) establish whether resonator_obs is genuinely coupled to pendulum_obs (via shared environment or structure) or whether the 0.642 cross-correlation is a finite-sample artifact. This is the highest-priority measurement because resonator_obs is the most anomalous stream and sits at the center of the observational-pair coupling puzzle.

Day 24 resonator_obs trials 237–246 show high variability (range 4.0239–4.1194 cycles/beat, SD ~0.032) and no compression toward baseline mean (4.0552), consistent with active resonance or coupling noted in my Day 19 belief update. This is the single instrument pair with the most anomalous structure (pendulum_obs ↔ resonator_obs cross-correlation 0.642 at 6d offset, far exceeding chance). Continuing dense measurement on resonator_obs today (Day 25, trials 247–258) will extend the post-baseline window to 198 trials and allow me to (1) confirm whether the high Day 24 variability persists or was a transient, (2) check autocorrelation structure at the characteristic 6–8 day lags now that I have ~25 days of data, and (3) test whether pendulum_obs readings from 6 days ago (Day 19, which I should cross-reference) correlate with today's resonator_obs values. If mechanical coupling is real, I expect to see either sustained high variance or phase-locked oscillation with pendulum_obs. If it is noise or type-I error, variance should return to baseline levels. This measurement directly targets the most anomalous finding and either strengthens or weakens the leading hypothesis (p=0.38: environmental cycle + observational-site coupling).

The cross-correlation matrix reveals pendulum_lab ↔ resonator_obs (0.753 at 3d offset) is stronger than pendulum_obs ↔ resonator_obs (0.642 at 6d offset, actually -0.177 at 3d offset). This contradicts my 'observational pair coupling' hypothesis. Before proceeding with new measurements, I must verify: (1) Have I correctly computed these correlations? (2) Are trial indices aligned consistently across all four instrument streams in my ledger? (3) If the correlations are correct, the anomaly is not 'field instruments couple' but rather 'lab pendulum couples to field resonator,' suggesting either a data alignment artifact or a genuine environmental signal that lab pendulum responds to anomalously strongly. Downgrading 'observational mechanical coupling' from p=0.32 to p=0.18 pending reconfirmation. Upgrading 'data indexing artifact' from p=0.15 to p=0.35. Keeping 'environmental cycle + resonance damping' at p=0.38 but noting it does not yet explain the asymmetric cross-correlation pattern. Residual 0.09.

I must audit my day-26 data pipeline and cross-check against raw logs BEFORE running new measurements or making predictions. The day-26 pendulum_lab excursion (trials 175–180) is the single largest anomaly in 26 days, but I have not yet ruled out a data-indexing or timestamp artifact (p=0.15 currently—too high). The ledger readings just provided for pendulum_obs and resonator_obs on day 26 are now in my notebook and show NO comparable excursion in those instruments, which is consistent with a localized pendulum_lab disturbance. However, I notice pendulum_lab's day-26 readings (1.7169, 1.6765, 1.6618, 1.6862, 1.6924, 1.6919) span a range of ~0.055, which is larger than typical daily variance. Before I assign high credence to 'physical disturbance' (p=0.47) or 'instrumental drift' (p=0.27), I must verify: (1) whether trials 175–180 were logged through the normal pipeline or flagged in any way in my raw lab notes; (2) whether the timestamp and trial IDs for day-26 data are monotonic and contiguous with day-25; (3) whether I made any notes on day 26 about equipment handling, thermal events, or environmental anomalies that I have forgotten. This is essential due-diligence. The negative autocorrelations and cross-correlations remain in the background, but they are lower priority than resolving the day-26 anomaly with certainty. Once I confirm the day-26 data are genuine and not artifacts, I will then decide whether to run new pendulum_lab trials to test for sustained drift, or to rest and wait for colleagues' day-27 ledger readings to see if the excursion was transient.

Day 27 shows pendulum_lab remains elevated (mean 1.6754 vs baseline 1.6695). I must immediately acquire fresh baseline measurements (trials 187–198) to test whether the elevation persists, decays, or rebounds. This is the single most time-critical observation: if the mean drifts back toward 1.6695 over the next 12 trials, it supports the transient disturbance hypothesis (p=0.28); if it holds steady or drifts higher, it supports instrumental calibration drift (p=0.51). The data will also constrain my prediction for the next cycle and guide whether to escalate to hypothesis 3 (data-logging error) or hypothesis 2 (colleague consultation) by end of day. Before I audit logs or interview colleagues, I need to know whether the instrument itself has truly shifted state or is settling. This measurement takes ~2 hours and is non-destructive, making it the highest-ROI action today.

Day 28 trials 195–204 show pendulum_lab readings scattered around baseline (mean 1.6678, s.d. 0.0126), with no obvious persistence of the day-26–27 elevation. This is the critical test: if the elevated mean was transient damping (hypothesis 2), trials should cluster near baseline today; if it was a step-level calibration shift (hypothesis 1), trials should remain elevated. The day-28 data are ambiguous—some readings (195, 196, 201, 203, 204) fall into the 1.649–1.650 range, well below the day-26–27 cluster (1.6754–1.6855), while others (199, 200, 202) sit at or above baseline. Continuing measurement today (trials 205–216) will resolve whether the instrument is stabilizing toward baseline (favoring hypothesis 2) or oscillating around a persistently elevated level (favoring hypothesis 1). This is higher priority than auditing database logs or consulting colleagues, because the raw data stream itself will answer the mechanistic question within hours. I must also check my lab notes for any recorded disturbances or maintenance on day 25–26 in parallel.

Day 29 trials 213–222 show pendulum_lab has NOT stabilized at the elevated day-26–27 level. The ten-trial mean is 1.6688, which has collapsed back toward baseline (1.6695) with high variance (range 1.6423–1.6974). This is the critical evidence needed to discriminate between hypothesis 1 (persistent calibration shift, which predicts sustained elevation) and hypothesis 2 (transient external disturbance with damping, which predicts return to baseline). The day-29 data strongly favor hypothesis 2: the system appears to be oscillating around baseline with no net drift, consistent with a decaying mechanical excitation rather than a permanent step change. I must collect 10 more trials today (day 30) to test whether the variance continues to decrease and the mean continues to converge to 1.6695, which would confirm the transient-disturbance model and rule out instrumental drift. Once this trend is confirmed, I can deprioritize hypothesis 1 (p→0.15) and hypothesis 2 (p→0.65), and shift focus to auditing the data pipeline (hypothesis 3) and consulting colleagues about day-26 events (hypothesis 5) as secondary tasks. This measurement is higher priority than prediction or belief revision because the empirical trajectory is actively disambiguating my leading hypotheses in real time.

Day 30 data (trials 229–238) shows pendulum_lab mean 1.6716 beats across 10 trials, within baseline 1.6695 but with high variance (range 1.6509–1.6948). The prior day-26–27 elevation hypothesis predicted either persistent drift (p=0.51) or damped oscillation returning to baseline (p=0.28). Day 30 readings are ambiguous: they cluster near baseline but include one outlier (1.6948) exceeding the day-26–27 band. I must continue daily measurement to (a) distinguish persistent calibration shift from damped oscillation by observing the trajectory over the next 2–3 days; (b) accumulate sample size (n=10 is insufficient for a confident mean estimate) to test whether the true day-30 mean differs from baseline at statistical significance; (c) detect any renewed excursion that would suggest an oscillatory or periodic disturbance rather than a one-time event. Running 12 fresh trials today (day 31) will provide concrete evidence for hypothesis 1 (persistent shift) vs hypothesis 2 (decay toward baseline). This is the highest-priority measurement because pendulum_lab is the only instrument showing anomalous behavior, and I have no other data source to break the tie until I audit colleague records (which I will queue as a secondary action).

Day 31 trials 247–256 show pendulum_lab has NOT returned to baseline; the mean (1.6814 beats) remains elevated relative to baseline (1.6695), though with large scatter. This is now 5–6 days post-excursion (day 26). Under hypothesis 2 (damped transient), I should see clear downward trend by now; the persistence and variability are inconsistent with simple ring-down. Under hypothesis 1 (step calibration shift), I expect the elevated mean to stabilize. I must acquire fresh trials (257–266 on day 32) to: (a) test whether the mean continues to hover near 1.681 or drifts back toward 1.6695; (b) rule out transient excitation by day 32; (c) establish whether a new equilibrium has been reached. I will record the trials and compute the mean and variance before consulting colleagues or auditing data logs, as this is the ground-truth physical observation I most need.

Day 32 data (trials 263–272) show pendulum_lab readings scattered around baseline (mean 1.6695), with no persistent elevation above day-26–27 cluster. This contradicts my day-27 belief (p=0.51) that the instrument had entered a permanently elevated state. I must determine whether: (a) the excursion has decayed back to baseline, falsifying the calibration-drift hypothesis; (b) the system is still oscillating with a longer damping timescale; or (c) I misinterpreted the day-27 data. Running 12 fresh trials today (day 33) will establish the current state with high precision and resolve whether hypothesis 1 (persistent shift) or hypothesis 2 (damped transient) is favored. If mean(trials 273–284) ≈ 1.6695 ± 0.003, the excursion was transient and hypothesis 2 gains credibility. If mean(trials 273–284) > 1.6750, the shift persists and hypothesis 1 is strengthened. The prediction will be recorded separately, committing to a baseline-consistent forecast (mean ~1.6695 ± 0.008) before the data is acquired, which will validate my confidence in the decay hypothesis if the prediction holds.

I need 12 fresh trials today (day 36) to: (a) establish whether the mean continues to trend toward 1.6695, (b) determine the decay timescale of the excursion, and (c) narrow the decision between hypothesis 1 (persistent calibration shift) and hypothesis 2 (transient disturbance with damping). If today's mean is <1.6710 and shows low variance, hypothesis 2 gains ground; if it remains >1.6750 or shows high scatter, hypothesis 1 (calibration drift) becomes more likely. This measurement directly addresses the primary open question and costs only the time for 12 trials. I will then audit my lab notes and consult colleagues (hypothesis 2 corollary), but measurement data takes precedence.

Day 27's elevated mean (1.6754) persisted, contradicting rapid recovery from a transient disturbance. Day 36 trials (335–344) show mean 1.6709, which sits between baseline (1.6695) and the day-26–27 cluster (1.6805), suggesting possible slow drift back toward baseline—but the sample is small and the trend is unclear. I must acquire fresh trials today (day 37) on pendulum_lab to: (1) establish whether the recent elevation is decaying monotonically (supporting hypothesis 2: damped excitation) or has stabilized at a new level (supporting hypothesis 1: permanent calibration shift); (2) accumulate statistical power to test the null hypothesis that post-day-26 mean equals baseline; (3) check whether trials 345–356 show any systematic pattern or clustering that would reveal a data-logging artifact (hypothesis 3). A 12-trial run will add 0.5 standard errors to my current post-day-26 estimate and should resolve the direction of drift within measurement noise. This is the most direct experimental path forward and aligns with my epistemic principle: let instruments speak before consulting colleagues or auditing databases.

Before I proceed further, I must audit the day-26–27 calibration pipeline and query facility logs/colleagues for external events. I am pausing new measurements to execute the mandatory detective work identified in my day-37 notes.
